paper_title: NitroFusion2: Bringing Adversarial Loss to the Text Stream of Multimodal Diffusion Transformers

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Adversarial diffusion distillation has conventionally relied on image features for discrimination. We revisit this choice for multimodal diffusion transformers (MMDiTs), whose text stream becomes image-dependent through joint attention. We introduce Text-Stream Adversarial Distillation (TSAD), which exploits intermediate text-token states as a new adversarial representation. Because the text stream has already read the image while remaining tied to the text condition, changing that condition changes what information it extracts from the image. Building on this property, we introduce Aspect-Cued Discrimination (ACD), which conditions the discriminator on different aspects of the sample, such as typography, objects, or style, to steer which properties are emphasized during adversarial training. Building on the expert-discriminator design of NitroFusion, we integrate TSAD and ACD in NitroFusion2. NitroFusion2 brings few-step distillation from the conventional 4-8-step regime down to just 1-2 steps at comparable quality. At one step, it produces sharp rendered text and rich fine-grained details, making one-step generation practical rather than merely a stress test for distillation. At two steps, it remains competitive across the evaluated benchmarks. These results establish the MMDiT text stream as a powerful and steerable representation for adversarial diffusion distillation.

sections.title:
BRINGING ADVERSARIAL LOSS TO THE TEXT STREAM
OF MULTIMODAL DIFFUSION TRANSFORMERS
sections.content: Dar-Yen Chen1,2 Yi-Zhe Song1 1SketchX, CVSSP, University of Surrey {d.chen, y.song}@surrey.ac.uk 2Turing Elite Research Labs ABSTRACT Adversarial diffusion distillation has conventionally relied on image features for discrimination. We revisit this choice for multimodal diffusion transformers (MMDiTs), whose text stream becomes image-dependent through joint attention. We introduce Text-Stream Adversarial Distillation (TSAD), which exploits intermediate text-token states as new adversarial representation. Because the text stream has already read the image while remaining tied to the text condition, changing that condition changes what information it extracts from the image. Building on this property, we introduce Aspect-Cued Discrimination (ACD), which conditions the discriminator on different aspects of the sample, such as typography, objects, or style, to steer which properties are emphasized during adversarial training. Building on the expert-discriminator design of NitroFusion, we integrate TSAD and ACD in NitroFusion2. NitroFusion2 brings few-step distillation from the conventional 48-step regime down to just 12 steps at comparable quality. At one step, it produces sharp rendered text and rich fine-grained details, making one-step generation practical rather than merely stress test for distillation. At two steps, it remains competitive across the evaluated benchmarks. These results establish the MMDiT text stream as powerful and steerable representation for adversarial diffusion distillation. sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Adversarial diffusion distillation is an effective approach to few-step generation [75]: discriminator heads distinguish reference samples from student samples using intermediate features of pretrained backbone, and the student is trained to fool them [6, 32, 58, 59]. The backbone may be an external encoder or the diffusion model itself. Nearly every part of that recipe has been revisited, from the objectives [74, 75] and training strategies [8, 53] to the discriminator design [6, 33, 58], except one: what the discriminator heads read. They read image features. We revisit this choice for multimodal diffusion transformers (MMDiTs). This choice was natural for earlier diffusion architectures. In cross-attention UNet [2, 49, 54, 55], the text embeddings used for conditioning remain image-independent throughout the denoising network. The architecture therefore does not maintain text-token hidden states that depend on the sample being processed. MMDiTs [9] change this premise. Through joint attention, intermediate text-token states repeatedly interact with image tokens and become dependent on the particular sample being processed [1, 11, 64]. The MMDiT text stream therefore exposes representation that conventional adversarial distillation has largely left unused. We exploit this representation with Text-Stream Adversarial Distillation (TSAD), which attaches lightweight discriminator heads to intermediate text-token states of the discriminator backbone. These heads operate on text-token representations that have already interacted with the image. This turns the text stream itself into discriminator representation. In joint attention, text tokens query image features, and what they gather is written back into their own states [11, 30, 64], so changing the text condition changes what the text stream extracts from the image. If the reference faithfully presents queried property, such as clear rendered text, the correct object colour, or particular visual style, the student must reproduce it well enough to fool the discriminator under the same emphasis. Building on this property, we introduce Aspect-Cued Discrimination (ACD). For each reference image, we construct an image-grounded structured caption with six fields: typography, object, style, background, action, and layout. At each training step, the discriminator is conditioned on either one valid aspect field or the full structured caption, while the student keeps its original prompt. The cue therefore steers what the text stream queries from the image and which aspects are emphasized by the adversarial signal. Building on the expert-discriminator design of NitroFusion [6], we introduce NitroFusion2, distilled from Z-Image-Turbo [77], extending adversarial discrimination to the MMDiT text stream through TSAD and ACD. Controlled ablations test these two design choices. Text-stream discrimination outperforms conventional image-stream discrimination across all evaluated benchmarks, while combining the two streams performs best on most metrics. Aspect cues further turn the discriminator into an expert on the selected aspect, improving performance on that property. Together, these designs enable substantial leap in one-step generation. At two steps, NitroFusion2 is competitive with alternatives [37] that use separate parameter sets for their two-step trajectories. In summary, our contributions are: We identify the text stream of MMDiTs as discriminative representation for adversarial diffusion distillation and introduce Text-Stream Adversarial Distillation, which applies discriminator heads to intermediate text-token states. We introduce Aspect-Cued Discrimination, which uses the discriminators text conditioning to steer which properties are emphasized by the text stream. We show that text-stream discrimination outperforms conventional image-stream discrimination across all evaluated benchmarks, and that aspect cues yield aspect-specific gains. Together, these advances bring few-step distillation from the conventional 48-step regime down to 12 steps at comparable quality. If this paper has one message, it is this: in an MMDiT, the text stream is no longer only conditioning. Once it reads the image, it becomes discriminative representation, opening new direction for adversarial diffusion distillation and allowing that discrimination to be steered toward specific aspects. 2 Preprint.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Few-Step Diffusion Models. Reducing diffusion sampling to few network evaluations has motivated large body of distillation work. Progressive Distillation [56] pioneered curriculum that halves the step count iteratively, later generalised to multistep targets [16]. Consistency models [61] and their variants [7, 24, 41, 42, 53, 60, 65] enforce self-consistency along the sampling trajectory, mapping any point on it directly to the endpoint. Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) [43, 75, 76] minimises divergence between student and teacher outputs, and has since been extended in several directions [3, 10, 20, 25, 29, 38, 40, 66, 68, 69, 74]. MeanFlow [12, 13] learns the average velocity across an interval. Self-adversarial fine-tuning has the model supply its own adversarial target [8, 36]. Despite this progress, oneand two-step generation remains challenging [8, 37]. Adversarial Diffusion Distillation. Adversarial objectives recover fidelity lost at low step counts. ADD [59] attaches lightweight discriminator heads to frozen DINOv2 encoder [47] in pixel space. LADD [58] moves discrimination into latent space, applying heads to the token sequence the teacher diffusion model emits after each attention block. NitroFusion [6] organises the critic as an ensemble of specialised expert heads in place of single scorer. Subsequent methods develop these designs across backbones and head architectures [3, 6, 7, 22, 32, 33, 66, 73, 75], and several train the critic on teacher generations in place of real images [3, 6, 22, 32, 37, 58]. Text-conditioned discrimination was developed earlier in text-to-image GANs [28, 45, 52, 57, 63, 72, 78]. GigaGAN [21] brings it to large-scale models, conditioning its discriminator on pooled global descriptor while its generator uses word-level cross-attention. Across these designs the text conditions the judgement while the features the discriminator reads come from the image. Text-Image Representations in Diffusion Models. Diffusion models develop rich text-image correspondences. In cross-attention UNets, word-level attention maps support attribution [35, 62], editing [18, 48], inference-time correction [5, 51], and segmentation [46, 70], while the text representation itself does not vary with the image. Joint attention in multimodal diffusion transformers [9] changes this. ConceptAttention [17] localizes concepts in attention outputs, while recent analyses show that text-stream positions absorb image content [30, 64], including in image-conditioned incontext generation [11], causally steer outputs [27], and support concept prediction from partially denoised states [1]. These representations have been used for analysis and inference-time control, attention-map supervision [23], and preference rewards [39], but not directly as the feature space for adversarial supervision.

We exploit this flexibility with Aspect-Cued Discrimination (ACD), which conditions the discriminator on one structured aspect of the sample at time. For each reference image, we construct six image-grounded aspect fields indexed by = {typography, object, style, background, action, layout}. We denote the text associated with aspect by ak. Their combination forms the full structured caption cfull. Fields whose content is absent from the image are left empty. The valid cue categories for sample are K(a) = {full} {k : ak = }. The student remains conditioned on the original prompt p, while the frozen discriminator backbone is conditioned on q. The same cue is used for the corresponding reference and student samples. Following the expert-head design of NitroFusion [6], the text-stream discriminator uses heads specific to cue categories. typography cue is scored by typography heads, an object cue by object heads, and likewise for the remaining aspects and the full caption. The image-stream heads remain shared across cues, while their input states still depend on through the conditioned MMDiT backbone. The sampled cue therefore affects text-stream discrimination in two coupled ways. It changes the text queries and hence the image information written into the text-token states, and it selects the corresponding aspect-specific text-stream heads. typography cue, for example, conditions the backbone on the rendered-text description and routes the resulting states to the typography heads, while an object cue uses the object description and object heads. Figure 3 qualitatively illustrates this cue-dependent attention. With the same image fixed, different aspect cues produce different image-to-text attention patterns; for example, the typography and object cues emphasize different regions associated with rendered text and foreground objects, the background cue shifts attention away from the foreground toward the surrounding scene, and the full caption spreads attention more broadly across the image. These patterns are consistent with ACD steering image-to-text attention through the discriminator cue. ACD requires no additional backbone evaluation and only selects the corresponding lightweight text-stream heads. 3.4 DATASET CONSTRUCTION We construct synthetic dataset of 100k reference images [3, 6, 22, 32, 37, 58] using Z-Image-Turbo [77] with twelve sampling steps, split evenly between English and Chinese prompts. For example, the typography field is populated only when visible text is present. We additionally verify that the resulting structured caption is consistent with the original prompt p. sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: Both our student and our discriminator backbone are initialized from Z-Image-Turbo [77], and the discriminator backbone is kept frozen throughout training. We evaluate NitroFusion2 on LongTextBench [14] in English and Chinese, OneIG-Bench [4], GenEval [15], and DPG-Bench [19]. We compare against few-step students of Z-Image: Z-Image-Turbo [77], TwinFlow [8], and Z-ImageTurbo++ [37]. Z-Image-Turbo++ uses step-decoupled weights, with separate model for each of its two steps. Its weights are not released, so we report its published two-step metrics but cannot evaluate it at one step or include it in our qualitative comparisons. Training details are given in Section and per-dimension benchmark breakdowns in Section B. All qualitative samples in this section are generated at 1024 1024. 4.1 QUALITATIVE RESULTS Figure 4 compares NitroFusion2 with Z-Image-Turbo and TwinFlow at one and two sampling steps. The clearest difference is in rendered text. At one step, NitroFusion2 already produces sharp, legible title, The Old Man and the Sea, while both baselines blur or distort the lettering. At two steps, NitroFusion2 also renders the much smaller author name, Ernest Hemingway, clearly. Because the discriminator is conditioned on the described text, the student must reproduce the glyphs it names, not merely produce sharp lettering. Beyond typography, NitroFusion2 already produces realistic, fine-grained details at one step, including sharp structure in hair, fur, foliage, water, and reflections. Figure 5 further shows that high-quality generation is available from the first step and remains stable as the sampling budget increases. Onestep generation can still struggle with complex scenes, but these errors are progressively alleviated with more steps; in these examples the visual differences beyond eight steps are small. 7 Preprint. At one step, NitroFusion2 leads all evaluated baselines across all five benchmarks. Compared with TwinFlow, it substantially improves LongText-EN and LongText-CN by 14.2 and 10.9 points, respectively, while also improving GenEval, DPG-Bench, and OneIG. The GenEval breakdown in Table 2 further shows that this advantage extends across compositional skills. NitroFusion2 leads five of six categories, with particularly strong results on singleand two-object generation, colors, and color attribution. At two steps, NitroFusion2 remains strong overall. It leads four of six GenEval categories and outperforms TwinFlow on both LongText splits. Z-Image-Turbo++ achieves higher scores on some metrics and uses two step-specific 6B parameter sets, 12B parameters in total, whereas single 6B NitroFusion2 model is used at any sampling step. Most notably, NitroFusion2 leads all evaluated benchmarks at one step. At that single step it also surpasses the eight-step Z-Image-Turbo reference on DPG-Bench (86.48 against 84.86) and is on par with it on GenEval (75.86 against 75.01), at one eighth the sampling cost, while substantial gap to that reference remains on text rendering. One step is also where the adversarial signal matters most, since the student cannot revise its output over later steps and must place all structure in single pass. 4.3 ABLATION STUDY We ablate the two components: first, which stream provides the adversarial representation; second, which cue conditions the shared discriminator backbone. All ablation runs are trained for 1,000 steps. Which stream should the discriminator read? Table 3 compares image-stream, text-stream, and joint discrimination. Text-stream discrimination alone outperforms conventional image-stream discrimination on every benchmark. Combining both streams further improves four of the five metrics, including both LongText splits, DPG-Bench, and OneIG. GenEval is the exception, where the textonly model performs best. These results isolate the contribution of extending adversarial discrimination to the text stream. Textstream supervision is stronger than image-stream supervision across all five metrics. Our approach retains both because the image-stream signal provides an additional gain on most metrics. Which cue should condition the discriminator? We next fix the joint textand image-stream discriminator and vary only the cue supplied to its shared backbone. Table 4 compares models trained with single typography, style, or object cue, the full structured caption, and ACD with all cues sampled uniformly. All settings use the same training data and discriminator architecture. Where Fig. 3 shows that the cue changes where the text stream reads, Table 4 asks whether that shows up in what the student learns. 8 Preprint. Image Text Text+Image Typography Style Object All cues Figure 6: Two-step ablative samples. Left: image-stream, text-stream, and joint discrimination. Right: models trained with individual typography, style, or object cues compared with the full sevencue ACD mixture. Among the single-aspect models, each cue performs best on the evaluation category associated with the aspect it names. The typography cue gives by far the strongest LongText scores, the style cue gives the strongest OneIG-Style score, and the object cue gives the strongest single-aspect results on both object-focused metrics. The full structured caption does not lead any targeted category. This targeted pattern indicates that changing the cue changes which properties receive the strongest adversarial supervision. Typography alone, for instance, exceeds the final model on LongText, because all of its adversarial supervision is spent on rendered text. Sampling across all cues produces broader effect. Rather than specializing in single property, the mixed cue policy balances supervision across different aspects. It does not maximize every targeted category, but gives the strongest OneIG-Style, DPG-Entity, and both alignment scores in the table. More importantly, the full ACD mixture outperforms the full structured prompt on six of seven metrics, supporting the benefit of decomposing the prompt into specialized aspect cues rather than conditioning on the full caption alone. In particular, the two alignment metrics are highest under the mixed cue policy rather than any single-aspect specialization. The qualitative ablations in Fig. 6 illustrate the same trends. On the left, image-stream discrimination struggles with rendered text and complex structure: it duplicates KYOTO and introduces artifacts around the cat, while text-stream and joint discrimination produce cleaner results. On the right, the effect of different ACD cues is visible across aspects. The typography cue produces the clearest menu text, while the object cue best preserves the requested sequence of colored balloons. Sampling across all cues performs well in both cases, illustrating the broader balance of the full ACD mixture.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION AND LIMITATIONS
sections.content: Our experiments show that MMDiT text-token states can serve as an effective adversarial representation. Text-Stream Adversarial Distillation (TSAD) exploits these states for supervision, with particularly strong gains in text rendering, while Aspect-Cued Discrimination (ACD) provides targeted control and better overall balance than full-prompt conditioning. Together, they enable NitroFusion2 to substantially narrow the gap between one-step and multi-step generation. The text stream is useful here not only because it carries image information, but because what it carries can be redirected by the conditioning, making it steerable representation rather than fixed one. Several limitations remain. Complex scenes are still challenging, particularly at one step, and sample diversity is reduced. ACD also exhibits seesaw effect across cues, where emphasizing one aspect can improve that property while weakening others. Our layer selection is supported empirically rather than established as optimal. These observations suggest several directions for future work. Better balancing the seesaw effect across cues may further improve ACD, while studying where and how text-stream information evolves across depth could lead to more effective discriminator designs. Which aspects make effective cues also remains an open question; the six fields used here are design choice. More broadly, text-stream states may provide useful supervision beyond adversarial distillation, opening wider direction for training and controlling multimodal diffusion models. 9 Preprint.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: In this work, we used generative AI tools and LLMs to generate synthetic data sets, implement methods, provide feedback on research methodology and experiments, and interpret results. We also used them to draft and edit parts of this paper and to create and modify its figures. We did not use them to propose or refine the hypotheses of this work or to develop its conceptual framework. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work: every reported number comes from run the authors launched and verified. The authors are responsible for all content in this paper, including anything produced with AI assistance.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: The method is defined in Sections 3.2 and 3.3 and the training objective in Section 3.5. Section gives the training setup. Section A.1 lists the seven cue categories and Section A.2 the layers each set of heads reads. Section sets out one full training step as pseudo-code. Dataset construction, including the annotation model and the six structured-caption fields, is described in Section 3.4. NitroFusion2 will be released publicly upon acceptance.

sections.title: A IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: We use Adam with β1 = 0.0, β2 = 0.9, no weight decay, learning rate of 5 105 and batch size of 256, on eight H100 GPUs. The final model is trained for 20,000 steps in two stages. The first 5,000 steps are off-policy. The remaining 15,000 are on-policy, where the students input is state rolled out along its own trajectory, and we set λfm = 0, dropping the flow-matching term. The discriminator heads follow the design of APT [33]. Following NitroFusion [6], the image stream and each cue carry pool of three heads rather than single head, and one head is drawn at random per step. We also refresh the heads periodically by re-initializing their weights, which reduces overfitting. A.1 THE CUE LIST Table 5 lists the seven cue categories and the text each one supplies to the discriminator. The structured caption they are drawn from is written by Qwen3.5-35B-A3B [50] from the reference image itself, so each field is detailed and closely aligned with that image. Cue Text the discriminator is conditioned on Table 5: The seven cue categories. Full caption Every field concatenated: the complete specification of the image. Typography The rendered text, transcribed line by line with each lines position and lettering. Populated only when the image contains visible text. Object Style The subject: what is depicted, with the counts and identities of the entities preserved. The palette, artistic medium and rendering treatment, describing how the image is rendered rather than what it shows. Background The setting the subject sits in: surroundings, surfaces, weather and ambient detail, excluding the subject itself. Action Layout What the subject is doing, or an explicit statement that the scene is static. Where elements sit in the frame and how they are placed relative to one another. A.2 CHOOSING WHERE THE HEADS READ We score each layer of the frozen backbone by how far cues attention map departs from the full captions. The full caption itself is scored by its mean departure from the other six cues. Cues separate more after layer 20, so the four best-scoring layers all fall in one band. We keep the two strongest and replace the others with the best-separating layer of the mid and of the early range, so head also reads coarser shared structure  (Table 6)  . The image stream gets no such selection: its states are not indexed by the cue, so there is no per-cue attention map to rank. We spread its taps evenly across depth instead, at layers 5, 13, 21 and 29. Table 6: Read layers per cue. Indices into the backbones 30 joint-attention layers. The selected taps lead on four of the five metrics, most clearly on Preprint. text rendering; GenEval is the exception. We did not sweep it further, so the choice is supported empirically rather than established as optimal. Table 7: Where the text-stream heads read. Trained for 1,000 steps and evaluated at 1 NFE. Figure 7 shows the qualitative comparison. At one step, only NitroFusion2 produces consistently sharp outputs across all three examples, preserving fine detail in the cherry-blossom branches, facial hair, and ornate headdresses. At two steps, the differences become smaller, while NitroFusion2 continues to produce fine-grained detail with 6B model, half the size of Krea 2 Turbo and less than third of Qwen-Image-2512 Turbo. Table 10 reports the quantitative results. At one step, NitroFusion2 leads four of the five benchmarks, trailing only on LongText-CN. At two steps, QwenImage-2512 Turbo leads on text rendering and Krea 2 Turbo on GenEval, while the three models are close on DPG-Bench and OneIG, leaving NitroFusion2 competitive with both larger models. 16 Preprint.
